title: Laws of Motion
topics: Force, inertia, and Newton's First Law of Motion
Linear momentum, Newton's Second Law, and Impulse
Law of conservation of linear momentum and applications
Equilibrium of concurrent forces and Lami's theorem
Static and kinetic friction, laws of friction, rolling friction
Dynamics of uniform circular motion and centripetal force
Vehicle on a level circular road and vehicle on a banked road
notes:
## 1. Newton's Laws and Inertial vs Non-Inertial Frames
* **First Law (Law of Inertia):** Defines inertial frames of reference. A body remains at rest or in uniform rectilinear motion unless acted upon by a net external force ($\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0 \iff \vec{a} = 0$).
* **Second Law:** The rate of change of linear momentum $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ equals the net external force:
  $$\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} + \vec{v}\frac{dm}{dt}$$
  For constant mass, $\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = m\vec{a}$.
* **Third Law:** Action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction ($\vec{F}_{AB} = -\vec{F}_{BA}$), have the **same physical nature**, act simultaneously, and **always act on two different bodies** (so they never cancel each other on a single Free Body Diagram).
* **Pseudo Force in Non-Inertial Frames:** In a frame accelerating at $\vec{a}_{\text{frame}}$ relative to an inertial frame, attach a fictitious force $\vec{F}_{\text{pseudo}} = -m\vec{a}_{\text{frame}}$ acting at the centre of mass of the observed body.

## 2. Constraint Relations for Strings, Pulleys, and Wedges
* **Inextensible String Constraint:** Along any taut inextensible string segment, the component of velocity and acceleration of both ends along the string must be equal, or equivalently $\sum \vec{T} \cdot \vec{x}_i = 0 \implies \sum \vec{T} \cdot \vec{v}_i = 0 \implies \sum \vec{T} \cdot \vec{a}_i = 0$.
* **Moving Pulley Relation:** If pulley $P$ moves with displacement/velocity/acceleration $a_P$ and the two ends of the string over it have $a_1$ and $a_2$ (all measured along the same axis), then:
  $$a_P = \frac{a_1 + a_2}{2}$$
* **Wedge-Block Normal Constraint:** The components of velocity and acceleration perpendicular to the contact surface must be identical for both bodies in contact ($v_{1\perp} = v_{2\perp}$ and $a_{1\perp} = a_{2\perp}$).

## 3. Friction: Static, Limiting, and Kinetic
* **Static Friction ($f_s$):** Self-adjusting tangential contact force opposing **impending relative motion**: $0 \le f_s \le f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$.
* **Kinetic Friction ($f_k$):** Constant magnitude opposing **actual relative velocity** between surfaces: $f_k = \mu_k N$ (typically $\mu_k < \mu_s$).
* **Angle of Friction ($\lambda$):** Angle made by the resultant contact force $R = \sqrt{N^2 + f_{s,\max}^2} = N\sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2}$ with the normal $N$; $\tan\lambda = \mu_s$.
* **Angle of Repose ($\theta_r$):** Minimum incline angle at which a block begins to slide under gravity alone: $\tan\theta_r = \mu_s$.
* **Minimum Force to Pull a Block on a Rough Horizontal Surface:** $F_{\min} = \frac{\mu_s mg}{\sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2}} = mg\sin\lambda$, applied at an upward angle $\theta = \lambda = \tan^{-1}(\mu_s)$.

## 4. Circular Turning of Vehicles
* Centripetal force is not a new fundamental force; it is the net radial inward force ($\sum F_{\text{radial}} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$) provided by tension, normal reaction, friction, or gravity.

formulas.title: Impulse-Momentum Theorem
formulas.explanation: States that the time integral of a force (impulse) equals the net vector change in linear momentum of the body.
formulas.assumptions: Measured in an inertial reference frame.
formulas.validityConditions: Always valid for both constant and time-varying forces.

Magnitude of acceleration of each block

formulas.title: Lami's Theorem for Three Concurrent Coplanar Forces in Equilibrium
formulas.explanation: For three coplanar concurrent forces in equilibrium (F_1 + F_2 + F_3 = 0), each force magnitude is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two forces.

variables.name: Magnitudes of the three concurrent forces
Angles directly opposite to F_1, F_2, F_3 respectively

formulas.assumptions: Forces are concurrent, coplanar, and in translational equilibrium (net force = 0).
formulas.validityConditions: Strictly valid for exactly 3 forces where α + β + γ = 2π rad (360°).

derivations.title: Maximum Safe Speed on a Banked Rough Circular Road
derivations.context: Determining the upper speed limit v_max for a vehicle on a road banked at angle θ with static friction coefficient μ_s.
steps: At maximum speed $v_{\max}$, the vehicle tends to skid **up** the banked incline, so limiting static friction $f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$ acts **down** the incline.
Resolve forces vertically (no vertical acceleration, $\sum F_y = 0$): $$N\cos\theta - f_{s,\max}\sin\theta = mg \implies N(\cos\theta - \mu_s\sin\theta) = mg$$

Resolve forces horizontally toward the centre of the circular turn ($\sum F_r = \frac{mv_{\max}^2}{r}$): $$N\sin\theta + f_{s,\max}\cos\theta = \frac{mv_{\max}^2}{r} \implies N(\sin\theta + \mu_s\cos\theta) = \frac{mv_{\max}^2}{r}$$
Divide the radial equation by the vertical equation and divide numerator and denominator by $\cos\theta$: $$\frac{v_{\max}^2}{rg} = \frac{\tan\theta + \mu_s}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}$$

derivations.title: Two-Block System on a Horizontal Surface with Friction Between Blocks
derivations.context: Criterion for whether two stacked blocks m_1 (top) and m_2 (bottom, on smooth ground) move together or slip when force F is applied to bottom block m_2.
steps: Assume both blocks move together with common acceleration: $$a_c = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2}$$
The only horizontal force accelerating the top block $m_1$ is static friction $f_s = m_1 a_c = \frac{m_1 F}{m_1 + m_2}$.
The maximum available static friction between the blocks is $f_{s,\max} = \mu_s m_1 g$.
For no slipping, require $f_s \le f_{s,\max}$: $$\frac{m_1 F}{m_1 + m_2} \le \mu_s m_1 g \implies F \le \mu_s(m_1 + m_2)g$$
If $F > \mu_s(m_1 + m_2)g$, slipping occurs: $a_1 = \mu_k g$ and $a_2 = \frac{F - \mu_k m_1 g}{m_2}$.

graphs.title: Friction Force (f) vs Applied Tangential Force (F_app)
graphs.curveType: Piecewise linear (45° line in static regime, slight drop at limiting threshold, horizontal line in kinetic regime)
graphs.equation: f = \begin{cases} F_{\text{app}}, & F_{\text{app}} \le \mu_s N \\ \mu_k N, & F_{\text{app}} > \mu_s N \end{cases}
graphs.slopeInterpretation: Slope is +1 (tan 45°) during the static regime because static friction equals the applied force; slope is 0 in the kinetic regime.
graphs.areaInterpretation: Not physically significant (force vs force plot).
graphs.physicalInterpretation: Shows that static friction is self-adjusting up to a peak threshold μ_s N, after which sliding begins and friction drops slightly to constant μ_k N.

graphs.title: Force (F) vs Time (t) Impulse Graph
graphs.slopeInterpretation: Slope dF/dt represents the rate of change of force (related to jerk da/dt = (1/m)dF/dt).
graphs.areaInterpretation: Signed area under the F-t curve equals net linear impulse J = Δp = m(v_f - v_i).
graphs.physicalInterpretation: Areas above the time axis increase momentum in the positive direction; areas below reduce it.

commonMistakes.topic: Using f = μ_s N Blindly in Static Cases
commonMistakes.mistake: Setting static friction equal to μ_s N whenever a block is at rest.
commonMistakes.correction: μ_s N is only the maximum possible (limiting) static friction. When a block remains in equilibrium, static friction equals whatever tangential force is needed to prevent slipping (f_s <= μ_s N).

commonMistakes.topic: Spring Cut vs String Cut Instantaneous Acceleration
commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming tensions in both strings and springs drop to zero instantaneously at the exact instant (t = 0+) another support is cut.
commonMistakes.correction: Ideal string tension changes instantaneously at t = 0+, whereas an ideal spring's tension T = kx cannot change instantaneously unless its length changes (unless the cut is made directly on the spring itself).

commonMistakes.mistake: Drawing both an outward centrifugal force mv^2/r and equating inward forces to mv^2/r in the same Free Body Diagram.
commonMistakes.correction: In the ground (inertial) frame, never draw centrifugal force; simply set ∑F_inward = mv^2/r. Use outward centrifugal force mv^2/r only in the rotating frame where radial acceleration is zero.

quickRevision: Apparent weight in a lift of mass m: N = m(g + a) when accelerating upward, N = m(g - a) when accelerating downward, and N = 0 in free fall.
Reading of a spring balance equals Tension T in its hook (in Newtons) or T/g (in kg-wt).
For a heavy uniform rope of mass M and length L pulled at one end by force F on a smooth horizontal floor, tension at distance x from the free rear end is T(x) = F(x/L).
Acceleration of a block sliding down a rough incline (θ > θ_repose) is a = g(sin θ - μ_k cos θ); when projected up the incline, retardation is a = g(sin θ + μ_k cos θ).
Rocket propulsion thrust force: F_thrust = -v_rel (dm/dt), and net equation of motion in gravity is m(dv/dt) = -v_rel(dm/dt) - mg.
